118 THIBTY-SECOND REPOET U. S. CIVIL SEBVICE COMMISSION. Greneral's Office. May 16, 1911, he was promoted to thepoeition of assifltant attorney, whicli he held until August 31, 1914, when he resigned. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of War, with the concurrence of the Civil Service Commission, in view of the statement of the Judge Advocate General that he believes Mr. Lemmond to be especially qualified for the position of law clerk by reason of hia education, training, and experience in legal work in the Department of Justice. November 10, 1914. Mr. W. T. Bateman may be appointed a watchman in a navy yard without compli- ance with the civil-service rules. This order is issued on the recommendation of the Secretary of the Navy, who says the case is a deserving one and that the general character of Mr. Bateman is such that he feels justified in recommending an exemption from the civil-service rules which will permit his employment in a navy yard so that he may be able to support his family. It appears that Mr. Bateman, seaman, formerly attached to the U. S. S. Foote, is at present a patient in the Naval Hospital, Washinrton, D. C. While visiting his family a l-pounder shell which he was snowing his child exploded and blew off his left hand. The Surgeon General of the Navy concurs in the recommendation of the Sec- retary of the Navy and says Mr. Bateman is a very deserving man. While Mr. Bate- man will be dischjEurged from the Navy for disability he can receive no pencdon, as hia disability was not incurred in the line of duty. The Civil Service Commission does not recommend the issuance of the order. November 10, 1914. Mrs. Alice B. Smith and Mrs. Eunice B. Neff may be appointed to clerical positions in the classified service of the Post Office Department without compliance with the civil-service rules. Mrs. Smith is the widow of John H. Smith, formerly a letter carrier at the Washing- ' ton post office, who served the Government continuously for 42 years and died as a result oi three strokes of paralysis (possibly due to exposure while serving his route as a carrier) and left a widow and two small children without means of support. Mrs. Neff is the widow of W. E. Neff, a former employee of the Post Office Depart- ment, who, after 10 years' faithful service, had a nervous breakdown, which resulted in insanity, and he recently died leaving three small children. Mrs. Neff is also the sole support of an aunt, who is an elderly woman. The Civil Service Commission does not reconunend the issuance of this order. November 10, 1914. Mr. Edwin B. Smith, who formerly held the position of clerk in the Interstate Com- merce Commission, may be reinstated to a classified position in the Post Office Depart- ment without regard to the length of his separation or the provisions of the civil-service rules requiring reinstatement in the same department. This order is issued on the recommendation of the Postmaster General because of Mr. Smith's previous efficient service in the Interstate Commerce Commission and the exceptional qualifications he has evinced in the performance of hia duties as confiden- tial clerk to the Postmaster General. November 11, 1914. Mrs. Ellen McCabe Bain may be reinstated as an operative in the Bureau of Engrav- ing and Printing without regard to the length of time she has been separated from the service. This order is issued on the recommendation of the Secretary of the Treasury, who states that Mrs. Bain served 11 years in the Bureau of Engraving and Printii^; that she rendered efficient service there; and it is believed that her reinstatement will be in the interests of the service. The Civil Service Commission states that in view of Mrs. Bain's 11 years of service, fairly recent separation, and the fact that she is not of advanced age, it will offer no objection to an Executive order being issued in her behalf. Novezuber 11, 1914. Mrs. Annie Day may be appointed to an appropriate position in the classified service at the Government Printing Office without regard to the civil-service rules. Mrs. Day is the widow of Joseph P. Day, a former employee of the Government Printing Office, who in 1908 received an injury in line of duty which hastened his death and for which he received no compensation, as the law granting such payments for injuries received in the line of duty did not become effective until nve weel^ thereafter. Mrs. Digitized by VjOOQIC
EXECUTIVE ORDEBS. 119 Day, with three small children, is now in destitute circumstances, and the Public Printer recommends that he be given authority to appoint her to a position in his ofl&ce. The Civil Service Commission is unable to concur in his recommendation. November 11, 1914. Mrs. Minnie D. Middle ton, of the District of Columbia, who served as a clerk in the War Department for a period of 12 years, may be reinstated in the classified service and appointed to a clerkship at ^00 in the Department of State, notwithstand- ing the lapse of more than one year since her separation from the service. Mrs. Middleton^s service in the War Department was faithful and efficient. She is at present employed upon the temporary force of the State Department dealing with the relief of American citizens abroad, and this order is issued upon the recommendar tion of the Secretary of State, who considers it in the interest of the public service. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in this recommendation. November 11, 1914. Horatio Whitted may be appointed to an appropriate position in the classified service without regard to the civil-service rules. Mr. Whitted was appointed as a la^ orer at $660 per annum on May 9, 1901, and assigned to the General i^and Office, where he still is employed. It appears that, although his principal duties were of the grade performed by classified employees, his name was erroneously omitted from the Bst of such employees who were classified by the Executive orders of January 12, 1905, and March 30, 19()5« and this order is issued on the recommendation of the Acting Secretary of the Interior to correct the error. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in this recommendation. November 16, 1914. William P. Fix may be appointed a skilled helper in the Bureau of Engraving and Printing without compliance with the civilnservice rules pertaining to that position. Mr. Fix was formerly a plate printer in the Bureau of Engraving and Printing, but on account of a physical disability for the proper performance of the work of a printer was compelled to resign. A physical examination given by the Civil Service Commis- sion develops the fact that he is able to perform duty as a skilled helper. This order la issued on the recommendation of the Secretary of the Treasury and is concurred in by the Civil Service Commission. November 17, 1914. Mrs. C. H. Brice may be appointed to a clerical position in the classified service without regard to the civil-service rules. This order is issued because of the fact that the main support of Mrs. Brice and her young daughter was provided monthly by her brother. Col. Franklin J. Moses, United States Marine Corps, who lost his life in the line of duty on September 26, 1914, in Vera Cruz. Mrs. Brice has passed a civil- service examination for clerk. The Civil Sersdce Commission does not recommend the issuance of an Executive order in this case. November 21, 1014. The two sons of Hon. Julian Uribe Uribe, first vice president of the Colombian House of Representatives, may be employed on irrigation projects in the United States without regard to the provisions of the civil-sendee rules, for the purpose of learning through such employment the theory and practice of irrigation with a view ultimately to introducing this branch of science into the Colombian Republic. This order is issued in accordance with the principles of international comity and is recommended by the Acting Secretary of the Department of the Interior and by the Secretary of State. The Civil Service Commission concurs with the Department of the Interior and the Department of State in recommending the issuance of the order. November 28, 1014. Miss Laura E. Scott may be appointed to a clerical position in the classified service of the Department of State without examination under the civil-service rules. This action is based upon the recommendation of the Acting Secretary of State because of Miss Scott's efficient service with several international arbitration com- missions, the exceptional qualifications she has e^dnced in the performance of her duties as confidential clerk to the Acting Secretary of State, and his representation that the loss of the services of Miss Scott, who has been with him in the capacity of confidential clerk for several years, would be a great inconvenience. The Civil Service Commission concurs in the recommendation of tins order. Digitized by Google
